summary: Summarizes requirements for resource priority mechanisms in SIP, meaning ways of prioritizing access to circuit-switched networks, end systems and proxy resources for emergency preparedness communications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3487 lists requirements for prioritizing some requests sent with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) during emergencies. It describes the resources and network arrangements involved, but does not specify the mechanism itself.

how can sip prioritize emergency calls

subtitle: Requirements for SIP-based priority mechanisms for emergency-preparedness communications.

tldr.problem: During emergencies, telephone circuits, IP bandwidth, gateways, receiving systems and SIP proxies may be congested. People coordinating response may need selected requests to receive preferred access.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets requirements for a SIP indication that invokes a named priority policy, and it lists requirements for authentication, authorization, privacy and resistance to denial of service.
tldr.outcome: It defines requirements rather than protocol features. It also says not all requirements can necessarily be met at once.

today: RFC 3487 is an Informational requirements document. It lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it in the unit metadata, and it does not specify a protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Emergency communications may compete for limited telephone circuits, IP bandwidth, gateways and computing capacity. RFC 3487 considers priority for real-time applications using the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), including voice, multimedia conferencing and instant messaging or presence.

The document sets requirements, not protocol features. It does not require the priority indication to be a SIP header, method or URI parameter, and it does not decide which communication method is best in an emergency.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC lists requirements for giving selected session-setup requests preferred access to scarce resources. It does not design the marker or dictate how a network must respond.

sections.title: Resources and Network Paths
sections.content:
The RFC names five resource types: gateway channels, circuit-switched network resources, IP network resources, receiving end-system capacity, and SIP proxy capacity. The document treats IP bandwidth and proxy overload as outside its protocol-requirements scope, and it does not require one mechanism to cover all five resource types.

It considers four combinations of IP and circuit-switched networks: IP end-to-end, IP to circuit-switched, circuit-switched to IP, and circuit-switched to IP and back to circuit-switched. It also distinguishes network models by how much they permit an application to change the network or its SIP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Priority may matter at several points, from a gateway channel to the receiving computer or phone system. A request may travel through Internet networks, telephone networks, or both.

sections.title: Requirements for a SIP Indication
sections.content:
The RFC calls a request carrying priority information a labelled request. Its indication should support different existing and future priority schemes, work across varied SIP networks, and be carried in a valid SIP request rather than through out-of-band signaling. Existing circuit-switched priority information should be translatable to SIP without loss when both circuit-switched sides use the same scheme.

The indication should name a policy rather than prescribe exact actions such as queue position or preemption; local policy determines those actions. The requirements also cover use with any SIP method and address, support for multiple schemes, discovery of supported schemes, testing outside emergencies, third-party call control and visibility to proxies. The RFC warns that these requirements may involve tradeoffs.
sections.plainLanguage: The priority marker should name a policy without telling each network exactly how to apply it. It should work across different networks and be testable before an emergency occurs.

sections.title: Authentication, Privacy and Abuse
sections.content:
A priority mechanism can be abused to obtain resources and deny service to others. The RFC therefore requires stronger authentication and authorization for priority requests than for ordinary requests, and says authentication should happen on the IP side rather than consuming scarce telephone circuits.

The security requirements also address replay, cut-and-paste and bid-down attacks, confidentiality of sensitive SIP fields, caller anonymity toward the destination, and denial of service. Unauthorized users should not be able to consume excessive network, storage or computing resources, and the mechanism should not amplify traffic toward an address whose reachability is unverified.
sections.plainLanguage: A caller must not be able to claim priority without permission. The design also needs to protect private call details and limit the resources that fake requests can consume.
